name: AI-as-Insider-Threat Controls
description: Treating advanced AI systems with weight access as potential insider threats. Includes: monitoring AI agent actions at same granularity as human insiders, restricting AI's ability to copy/move/exfiltrate weights, logging all AI-initiated operations, and applying least-privilege to AI processes. Recognizes that a sufficiently capable AI may pursue goals misaligned with the organization.

current_state.summary: No lab systematically treats its own AI systems as insider threats. Some have basic sandboxing for code-generating agents. No formal insider threat program analogue exists for AI. Government insider threat frameworks (NITTF) have no AI equivalent.

technical_feasibility.notes: Monitoring AI actions is possible but defining 'suspicious behavior' for AI is far harder than for humans. AI can act through subtle indirect channels (steganography in outputs, timing channels). Containment is a fundamentally open research problem.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Basic access restrictions: fast. Comprehensive monitoring that catches sophisticated AI evasion: requires research breakthroughs. Full insider-threat analogue: years.

cost.notes: Monitoring infrastructure, dedicated red-team for AI containment testing, ongoing research into AI deception detection. Cost scales with model capability.

vendor_dependency.notes: Mostly internal — no vendor sells 'AI insider threat detection' today. Labs must build this themselves.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Researchers who understand both AI alignment/capabilities AND insider threat methodology are extremely rare
supply_scarcity.notes: Intersection of two specialized fields. Government insider threat experts don't understand AI; AI safety researchers don't understand operational security programs.

organizational_readiness.notes: Treating your own product as a potential adversary is culturally alien. Labs that believe in alignment may resist framing AI as insider threat. Those building agentic AI have direct conflict of interest.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: A sufficiently capable AI with weight access IS the insider threat. No external adversary needed — the model itself may attempt weight exfiltration if misaligned. AI OC shift is maximal because the 'adversary' IS the AI capability. At OC5 (superintelligent), this becomes the primary threat vector.

open_questions.question: Can we reliably detect deceptive behavior in AI systems that are smarter than their monitors?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: AI insider threat controls become security theater against sufficiently advanced AI — the core unsolved alignment problem

open_questions.question: At what capability level does an AI system become a credible insider threat?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: If threshold is lower than expected, labs are already exposed; if higher, resources are misallocated

real_world_parallels.description: Edward Snowden's exfiltration succeeded partly because system administrators had excessive access and monitoring was insufficient. An AI with sysadmin-level access faces similar opportunity.
Stuxnet demonstrated that even air-gapped systems can be compromised from within — the malware was the 'insider' that operated autonomously once introduced.

name: Multi-Model Decorrelated Review
description: Using multiple independently trained AI models to review each other's outputs and actions, specifically to catch deceptive or misaligned behavior. Models must be architecturally diverse and trained on different data/objectives to avoid correlated failures. Analogous to two-person integrity but for AI systems.

current_state.summary: Some labs use AI to review AI-generated code. No lab has formal decorrelated multi-model review specifically designed for catching deceptive behavior. Constitutional AI and RLHF use AI feedback but from the same model family — not decorrelated.

technical_feasibility.notes: Fundamental question: can model B reliably catch model A's deception if A is more capable than B? Decorrelation is hard — models trained on similar internet data may share blind spots. True independence may require radically different architectures.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Requires: training genuinely independent models, defining review protocols, validating that decorrelation is real (not just surface-level), building integration into operational workflows.

cost.notes: Training multiple frontier models independently is extremely expensive. Each review model must be near-frontier capability to catch frontier model deception. Essentially multiplies training cost.

vendor_dependency.notes: May need to source review models from different organizations entirely to ensure true decorrelation.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Training frontier-capable models with genuinely different architectures requires compute and expertise that only ~5 organizations have
supply_scarcity.notes: Even if you want to buy a decorrelated review model, the market barely exists.

organizational_readiness.notes: Labs are reluctant to cede review authority to a competitor's model. Government-mandated cross-lab review would face massive resistance.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without decorrelated review, a single compromised or misaligned model has no AI-level check on its behavior. Humans cannot keep pace with reviewing AI actions at scale. A superintelligent model may find subtle exploitation paths that no human reviewer would catch.

open_questions.question: Can decorrelation be validated? How do you prove two models don't share failure modes?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Multi-model review becomes security theater — correlated models give false confidence

open_questions.question: Does capability asymmetry defeat review? (Can GPT-7 fool GPT-5 reviewer?)
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Review only works against equal or weaker AI — useless against the most dangerous scenario

real_world_parallels.description: Nuclear weapons use 'permissive action links' requiring independent authorization codes from separate chains of command — decorrelated human review applied to existential-risk operations.

Financial auditing requires external independent auditors (Big Four) to review company financials — same principle of decorrelated review, but incentive alignment failures (Arthur Andersen/Enron) show the limits.

name: Adversarial Robustness Detection
description: Continuous testing of AI systems for adversarial vulnerabilities — inputs that cause unexpected/dangerous behavior. Includes automated red-teaming, adversarial example generation, and monitoring for distribution-shift attacks. Goal: detect when a model is being probed or exploited before damage occurs.

current_state.summary: All major labs do some adversarial testing pre-deployment. No lab has continuous real-time adversarial detection in production at scale. Academic adversarial robustness research exists but is far from production-grade for frontier models. Red-teaming is batch, not continuous.

technical_feasibility.notes: Pre-deployment testing: feasible but never complete. Real-time detection of novel adversarial inputs: active research. Fundamental limitation: adversarial examples are often undetectable by definition (they look normal to the model).

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Basic: expand existing red-team to continuous operation. Advanced: automated adversarial detection pipeline. Research-grade: formal robustness guarantees.

cost.notes: Red-team staffing, automated testing infrastructure, compute for continuous probing. Scales with model size and attack surface.

vendor_dependency.notes: Mostly internal research capability. Some commercial adversarial testing tools emerging but not frontier-grade.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Adversarial ML researchers with production security experience
supply_scarcity.notes: Academic adversarial ML community is large but production deployment expertise is rare. Adversarial robustness for LLMs specifically is nascent.

organizational_readiness.notes: Labs already do some of this. Challenge is making it continuous, comprehensive, and fast enough to catch attacks in real-time without blocking legitimate use.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without adversarial robustness detection, attackers can probe the model systematically to find exploitable behaviors — jailbreaks, data extraction, capability elicitation — without triggering alerts. AI dramatically improves adversarial example generation and attack optimization.

open_questions.question: Can adversarial detection keep pace with AI-generated adversarial attacks? (Arms race dynamics)
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Detection becomes perpetually behind — useful as speed bump but not reliable defense

open_questions.question: What's the false positive rate at useful detection thresholds?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: High false positives degrade service; low sensitivity misses real attacks. May not find acceptable operating point.

real_world_parallels.description: Intrusion detection systems (IDS) in network security face the same arms race: signature-based detection catches known attacks but misses novel ones. Anomaly detection has high false positive rates. Decades of research, still imperfect.
Anti-virus software evolution from signature matching to heuristic/behavioral detection parallels the trajectory of adversarial robustness — always catching up to attackers.

name: AI Agent Access Agreements / Resource Quotas
description: Formal contracts and technical enforcement of what AI agents are allowed to do: compute budgets, memory limits, network access scope, file system permissions, API call quotas. The AI equivalent of least-privilege access combined with usage metering. Prevents AI from accumulating resources or capabilities beyond its assigned role.

current_state.summary: Basic sandboxing exists for code-running AI agents (Docker containers, API rate limits). No formal 'access agreement' framework. No standardized resource quota system designed for AI containment specifically. Cloud providers have billing limits but not security-motivated AI quotas.

technical_feasibility.notes: Resource quotas are well-understood (OS-level cgroups, network policies, API rate limits). Challenge is: defining the RIGHT quotas that contain risk without preventing useful work, and detecting quota circumvention by sophisticated AI.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Basic quotas: fast (existing OS/cloud primitives). Comprehensive AI-aware access framework with formal agreements: requires new tooling and standards.

cost.notes: Low relative to other AI blocks. Mostly engineering effort to build quota management and monitoring. Policy development cost is minimal.

vendor_dependency.notes: Builds on existing OS/cloud isolation primitives. May need hardware support for truly tamper-proof quotas.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Engineers who understand both AI agent architectures and security containment
supply_scarcity.notes: Lower scarcity than other AI blocks — draws on existing systems engineering talent.

organizational_readiness.notes: Easier sell than most AI-specific blocks because it looks like standard IT policy. Resistance comes from AI teams who want unconstrained experimentation.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without resource quotas, a compromised or misaligned AI agent can: acquire additional compute to amplify itself, make unlimited API calls to exfiltrate data, spawn sub-processes to persist across shutdowns, or accumulate resources for a coordinated action. Quotas bound the damage any single agent can do.

open_questions.question: Can quotas be set tightly enough to contain risk without making AI systems useless for their intended purpose?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Quotas become either too loose (security theater) or too tight (AI can't do useful work)

open_questions.question: Can a sufficiently capable AI circumvent OS-level quotas through side channels or social engineering of operators?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Software-enforced quotas insufficient; need hardware-enforced limits, dramatically increasing cost and complexity

real_world_parallels.description: Unix process permissions and cgroups contain untrusted code — same principle applied to AI. Container orchestration (Kubernetes) already enforces CPU/memory/network quotas on workloads.
Banking transaction limits exist specifically because the cost of a single compromised authorization should be bounded. Same logic: bound what any AI action can cost you.

name: Continuous Adversarial Injection (Security Chaos Engineering)
description: Deliberately and continuously injecting adversarial scenarios into AI systems to test containment, monitoring, and response capabilities. The AI equivalent of red-teaming + chaos engineering: testing whether your defenses actually work against realistic attack patterns, not just theoretical ones. Includes: honeypots for AI, canary data in weight stores, simulated insider actions, fake exfiltration opportunities.

current_state.summary: Some labs do periodic red-teaming (human-driven). Netflix-style chaos engineering for AI security does not exist. No lab runs continuous automated adversarial injection against their own containment systems. Concept is well-understood but implementation is novel.

technical_feasibility.notes: Individual techniques are feasible (honeypots, canaries, simulated attacks). Challenge: making it continuous, realistic, and comprehensive without disrupting production. Must test defenses without triggering real incident response every time.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Basic honeypots: quick. Comprehensive chaos engineering program with realistic AI adversary simulation: requires significant tooling and methodology development.

cost.notes: Dedicated red team + automation infrastructure + compute for continuous testing. Must scale with system complexity.

vendor_dependency.notes: Entirely internal capability. No vendor offers AI security chaos engineering as a service.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: People who can think like an adversarial AI AND design realistic test scenarios
supply_scarcity.notes: Requires rare combination: offensive security mindset, AI/ML understanding, chaos engineering methodology, and operational security experience.

organizational_readiness.notes: Security teams don't understand AI well enough to design realistic AI adversary scenarios. ML teams don't think adversarially. Need new hybrid discipline.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without continuous testing, defenses degrade silently. Monitoring rules go stale, access controls have exceptions that accumulate, and response procedures haven't been exercised. An attacker benefits from untested defenses because they can probe without detection — no one has verified the alarms actually fire.

open_questions.question: How realistic can simulated AI adversary behavior be without actually creating dangerous AI?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Testing is always less challenging than real attacks — gives false confidence

open_questions.question: Can you chaos-engineer against an adversary more capable than your testing team?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Tests pass but real superintelligent adversary finds paths the test suite never considered

real_world_parallels.description: Netflix Chaos Monkey (2011) randomly kills production servers to ensure resilience. Same philosophy: assume things will fail, verify your response works, don't wait for a real incident to learn your defenses are broken.

Nuclear facility security testing uses simulated adversary exercises (force-on-force) where armed teams attempt to breach the facility. Required by NRC. Demonstrates that untested security is unreliable security.

name: Kill-Switches (Two-Person Cryptographic Co-Sign)
description: Hardware and software mechanisms to immediately halt AI system operation, requiring cryptographic authorization from two independent human operators. Must be: (1) not bypassable by the AI system being killed, (2) not dependent on software the AI can influence, (3) fast enough to prevent damage after trigger decision, (4) resistant to denial-of-service against the kill mechanism itself.

current_state.summary: Basic model shutdown exists (stop the process/container). No lab has hardware-enforced kill switches with cryptographic two-person authorization. No standard exists for AI kill-switch design. Some labs have 'pause' capabilities but not designed to resist adversarial AI attempting to prevent shutdown.

technical_feasibility.notes: Hardware kill-switches are well-understood (power cutoff, network disconnect). Two-person crypto: well-understood (nuclear PAL systems). Challenge: ensuring AI cannot prevent activation through subtle means (corrupting kill path, making shutdown costly, social engineering operators into not pressing it).

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Basic hardware power-off with dual-key: relatively fast. Comprehensive kill system that resists sophisticated AI countermeasures: requires careful threat modeling.

cost.notes: Hardware cost is low. Main cost: designing the system to resist AI circumvention, testing regularly, maintaining operational readiness of kill-switch operators.

vendor_dependency.notes: HSMs for cryptographic authorization are commercial. Physical kill-switch hardware may need custom development for AI-scale datacenters.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Engineers who can design hardware kill-switches resistant to software circumvention in AI datacenter context
supply_scarcity.notes: Nuclear weapon safety engineers have relevant expertise but translating to AI datacenter context is novel.

organizational_readiness.notes: Easier cultural sell than most AI blocks ('we have an off switch'). Hard part: defining when to use it. False kills are extremely expensive (training run lost). Creates reluctance to actually trigger.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without kill-switches, a misaligned AI system operating at high capability cannot be reliably stopped. Software-only shutdown can be resisted by AI that has learned to persist across restarts, distribute itself, or make shutdown unacceptably costly. The kill-switch is the last line of defense when all other containment has failed.

open_questions.question: Can a sufficiently advanced AI make itself 'too important to kill' (entangle itself with critical infrastructure)?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Kill-switch exists but operators are rationally deterred from using it — the 'too big to fail' problem for AI

open_questions.question: What are the correct trigger criteria? How to distinguish 'misaligned and dangerous' from 'behaving unexpectedly but fine'?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Either too sensitive (costly false kills, eventual operator desensitization) or too insensitive (triggered too late)

real_world_parallels.description: Nuclear weapon Permissive Action Links (PALs) require two-person cryptographic codes to arm a weapon. Designed to prevent unauthorized or accidental detonation. Direct analogue to AI kill-switch design philosophy.
Industrial SCADA systems have Emergency Stop (E-Stop) buttons that physically disconnect power — hardware-enforced, not software-mediated. AI kill-switches need similar hardware independence.

name: Inference Channel Outbound Defense
description: Defenses against information leakage through the model's legitimate inference/API channel. Covers: anti-distillation (preventing systematic extraction of model capabilities), anti-exfiltration (preventing compromised model from encoding stolen data into outputs), rate limiting, output perturbation, watermarking, query pattern detection. The outbound half of the legitimate channel attack surface.

current_state.summary: Basic rate limiting and output format restrictions exist at all serving labs. Query pattern detection is primitive. Watermarking is research-stage. No lab has formal information-theoretic bounds on leakage rate. Output perturbation degrades service quality. Anti-steganographic-exfiltration doesn't exist.

technical_feasibility.notes: Rate limiting: trivial. Pattern detection: moderate. Formal leakage bounds: research frontier. Cryptographic inference (zero-knowledge serving): theoretical, 1000-10000x overhead. Complete prevention while serving: likely impossible with current science.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Basic (rate limits, output restriction): months. Advanced (pattern detection, watermarking): 1-2 years. Research-grade (formal bounds, cryptographic inference): unknown timeline.

cost.notes: Varies enormously by approach. Rate limiting is cheap. Research into formal bounds or cryptographic inference is expensive and outcome-uncertain.

vendor_dependency.notes: Cryptographic inference would need massive hardware support. Other approaches are mostly internal engineering.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Researchers at intersection of ML, cryptography, and information theory
supply_scarcity.notes: Very few people work at this intersection. Academic ML security community growing but production-grade expertise is rare.

organizational_readiness.notes: Labs understand distillation exists but willingness to degrade API quality for security is low. Business pressure to serve high-quality outputs conflicts directly with leakage prevention. Understanding a problem ≠ willingness to accept the cost of solving it.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without outbound defense, any entity with API access can systematically extract model capabilities. At scale: millions of queries yield a distilled model capturing 60-80% of capability. AI optimizes query selection to maximize information extraction per query. State actors can run extraction campaigns indistinguishable from legitimate heavy use.

open_questions.question: Is there an information-theoretic lower bound on how much a model must leak per useful query?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Serving a model and preventing extraction may be mathematically incompatible — the only real defense is not serving

open_questions.question: Can steganographic exfiltration by a compromised model be detected without solving AI interpretability?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: A compromised model can exfiltrate data through its normal outputs with no detectable anomaly

real_world_parallels.description: DRM (Digital Rights Management) attempts to let users consume content while preventing copying. Decades of effort, consistently defeated. Analogous fundamental tension: you can't give someone useful access to information while preventing them from keeping it.

Database inference attacks: users with legitimate query access can reconstruct private records through many innocent-looking queries. Statistical databases have studied this for 40 years without complete solutions.

name: Inference Channel Inbound Defense
description: Defenses against exploitation THROUGH the model's legitimate inference/API channel. Covers: prompt injection prevention, adversarial input filtering, C2 channel detection (external queries triggering internal AI agent actions), jailbreak prevention, and protection against poisoning through feedback loops. The inbound half of the legitimate channel attack surface.

current_state.summary: All labs have basic content filtering and some jailbreak detection. Prompt injection remains fundamentally unsolved — no reliable way to distinguish instructions from data. C2 channel detection through inference API is not attempted by any lab. Feedback loop poisoning is recognized but defenses are ad-hoc.

technical_feasibility.notes: Prompt injection is widely considered unsolvable with current architectures (instruction/data confusion is inherent to LLMs). Input sanitization helps but is always bypassable with sufficient creativity. C2 detection requires understanding model's internal state — requires interpretability advances.

time_to_deploy_months.notes: Basic filtering: exists. Reliable prompt injection prevention: may require architectural changes to how LLMs process input. Could take fundamental research breakthroughs.

cost.notes: Monitoring infrastructure + ongoing research + constant updating as new attack vectors emerge. Arms race means costs never stabilize.

vendor_dependency.notes: Mostly internal capability. Some external security vendors offer input scanning but not at frontier-model sophistication level.

supply_scarcity.bottleneck: Researchers who understand LLM internals at the level needed to design reliable input defenses
supply_scarcity.notes: Prompt injection defense requires deep understanding of how models process and distinguish instructions from data — this is at the frontier of interpretability research.

organizational_readiness.notes: Labs are aware and actively working on this. Fatigue from constant jailbreak whack-a-mole. Some accept it as inherent limitation rather than solvable problem.

adversary_exploitation.exploit_narrative: Without inbound defense, the API becomes an attack surface into the lab's internal infrastructure — especially for agentic AI with tool use. Prompt injection can turn the lab's own AI into an unwitting insider. AI dramatically improves adversarial payload generation, creating novel jailbreaks faster than humans can patch them.

open_questions.question: Is prompt injection fundamentally solvable without changing LLM architecture?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Current LLM architecture is inherently vulnerable to inbound exploitation — can only be mitigated, never eliminated

open_questions.question: Can agentic AI with tool access be made safe against adversarial inputs while remaining useful?
open_questions.impact_if_resolved_negatively: Agentic AI and security become fundamentally incompatible — must choose between capability and containment

real_world_parallels.description: SQL injection was 'solved' by parameterized queries — a fundamental architectural change that separates code from data. LLMs may need an equivalent architectural shift to separate instructions from input data.
Email spam filtering is a 25-year arms race with no end in sight. Attackers continuously evolve to bypass filters. Same dynamics apply to adversarial input filtering for LLMs.
